- `patent-dev/uspto-odp` — Complete Go client library for the USPTO Open Data Portal API. 15 stars. · ODP is new (it replaced PatentsView in March 2026) so mature clients are scarce. This one is written against the current API, unlike every PatentsView wrapper on GitHub, which now targets a dead endpoint.
- `patent-dev/epo-ops` — Go client for the EPO Open Patent Services v3.2 API. · Implements the OAuth2 consumer-key flow and, importantly, the fair-use throttling — the 403 'Fair Use policy' rejection observed in this research is the failure mode this library is built to avoid.
- `alex9smith/gdelt-doc-api` — Python client for the GDELT DOC 2.0 API with filter construction and article/timeline retrieval. · GDELT's query syntax is idiosyncratic and its rate limit is 1 request per 5 seconds (verified live). This wrapper handles both. Pair with linwoodc3/gdeltPyR for the raw 15-minute CSV path, which is the one that actually scales.
- `fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-website` — The React front end for USAspending.gov. 287 stars. · A working reference implementation of a government-data research panel: how they paginate around the 10,000-record cap, how they structure award-search filters, and how they render award modification timelines.
- `blencorp/capture-mcp-server` — MCP server integrating SAM.gov, USASpending.gov and related federal contracting sources into one tool surface. 34 stars. · Already joins the pre-award (SAM.gov) and post-award (USAspending) views of the same contract, which is the join a 'will X win the contract' market needs. Also shows how to live within SAM.gov's 1,000/day non-federal ceiling.
- `marc-shade/world-intel-mcp` — 120-tool MCP server for real-time global intelligence spanning markets, SEC filings, conflict and more. 649 stars. · Closest existing thing to the 'God's-eye' aggregator concept. Worth mining for its source list and for which free endpoints it found still working — but audit every feed it claims, since aggregator repos routinely carry dead endpoints for years.
- `riemannzeta/patent_mcp_server` — MCP server for USPTO data, updated for the ODP migration. · Documents the PatentsView-to-ODP key migration explicitly — previously-issued PatentsView keys do NOT work against ODP, which is the first thing that breaks when porting old patent code.

---

### Energy, Commodities, Mining & Minerals

#### CORE

**EIA Open Data API v2** — US Energy Information Administration `LIVE`

- The single richest free energy dataset on earth. Hourly US grid demand/generation/interchange by balancing authority (EIA-930), weekly petroleum stocks (crude, gasoline, distillate, Cushing), weekly natural gas storage by region, monthly/annual production for crude, gas, coal, nuclear, renewables, refinery utilization, imports/exports by country, electricity retail prices, STEO forecasts, and coal mine-level production. Hundreds of routes under a uniform facet/frequency query grammar.
- Docs: https://www.eia.gov/opendata/documentation.php
- Auth: free API key (instant self-service registration, email only) | Limits: No hard published quota. EIA guidance: sustained rate under ~9,000 requests/hour and burst under 5 requests/second avoids throttling. Hard response caps: 5,000 rows per JSON request, 300 rows per XML request; paginate with offset/length. History depth varies by series — many series go back to the 1970s-1980s, EIA-930 hourly from July 2015.
- Latency: hourly (EIA-930 grid, ~1-2h lag); weekly (petroleum Wed 10:30 ET, gas storage Thu 10:30 ET); monthly for most production series | Format: REST JSON (also XML, CSV)
- Relevance: CORE pricing input for: weekly crude/gasoline/distillate inventory-build contracts, Cushing stock levels, natural gas storage injection/withdrawal surprise vs consensus, US crude production crossing round numbers, monthly/annual renewable share thresholds, coal retirement counts, and peak-load records by ISO. Almost every US energy contract resolves against an EIA print.

**EIA Bulk Download + Grid Monitor six-month CSVs** — US Energy Information Administration `LIVE`

- Backfill path that bypasses the 5,000-row API cap. api.eia.gov/bulk/*.zip ships whole series families as one archive. The Grid Monitor six-month CSVs (EIA930_BALANCE_YYYY_Jan_Jun.csv, EIA930_SUBREGION_*.csv) ship every hour for every balancing authority with demand, demand forecast, net generation, total interchange, adjusted/imputed variants, and net generation split by 16 fuel types including battery storage and solar-with-storage.
- Docs: https://www.eia.gov/opendata/bulkfiles.php
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no documented request quota. Files are large (hundreds of MB per six-month balance file) — practical limit is your bandwidth. History: EIA-930 from July 2015 forward.
- Latency: bulk files refreshed daily; six-month CSVs updated continuously within the current half-year | Format: ZIP of JSON (bulk), CSV bulk (Grid Monitor)
- Relevance: CORE for building the historical base your forecast model and error bars are fitted on. You cannot compute a station's or a BA's historical forecast error without this. Directly prices peak-demand-record, fuel-mix-share and negative-price-hour-count contracts.

**ENTSO-E Transparency Platform RESTful API** — ENTSO-E (European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity) `LIVE`

- The EU equivalent of EIA-930, and legally mandated so coverage is near-complete. Actual and forecast load, actual generation per production type and per generating unit, installed capacity, day-ahead and intraday prices per bidding zone, cross-border physical flows and scheduled commercial exchanges, net transfer capacity, balancing reserves and imbalance prices, and — critically — planned and forced outages of generation units and transmission assets with capacity and expected restoration time.
- Docs: https://documenter.getpostman.com/view/7009892/2s93JtP3F6
- Auth: free security token — register on transparency.entsoe.eu then email transparency@entsoe.eu with subject 'RESTful API access'; granted within ~3 working days | Limits: 400 requests per minute per API token (per token, not per IP). Exceeding it triggers a temporary ban with automatic unban after ~10 minutes. Query window caps vary by document type (commonly 1 year per request for A65/A75 series). History generally from 2015.
- Latency: 15-minute to hourly depending on document type; outage notices near-realtime (urgent market messages) | Format: REST returning XML (ENTSO-E schema); some endpoints support ZIP
- Relevance: CORE for European power. The outage endpoints are the highest-alpha surface here — a forced nuclear or interconnector outage published as an urgent market message moves day-ahead prices before the market fully reprices. Prices EU power price threshold contracts, French nuclear availability contracts, German negative-price-hour counts, and gas-to-power switching.

**LBMA Precious Metal Price JSON** — London Bullion Market Association / ICE Benchmark Administration `LIVE`

- The actual benchmark fixings that physical precious metal contracts settle against, as plain JSON arrays with no key. One file per metal/session: gold_am, gold_pm, silver, platinum_am, platinum_pm, palladium_am, palladium_pm. Each record is {d: date, v: [USD, GBP, EUR]}. Gold history runs unbroken from 1968-04-01 to the present session.
- Docs: https://www.lbma.org.uk/prices-and-data/precious-metal-prices
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, no published rate limit. Full history in a single response — gold_pm.json is ~58 years of daily fixings, silver confirmed current through 2026-09-18. Files are a few hundred KB; cache them, do not poll aggressively.
- Latency: twice daily (10:30 and 15:00 London for gold; 12:00 London for silver); published within minutes of the auction | Format: REST JSON (static file)
- Relevance: CORE and criminally underused. This is the settlement source, not a scraped proxy — gold-above-$X, silver-above-$X and gold/silver-ratio contracts resolve on these exact numbers. The 58-year history makes it the best free training set for metals volatility and threshold-crossing base rates anywhere.

**USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries + National Minerals Information Center** — US Geological Survey `LIVE`

- The authoritative global minerals reference. Annual per-commodity chapters for ~90 minerals covering world mine production by country, reserves by country, US import reliance percentage, apparent consumption, price series, recycling rates, and the events/trends narrative. The machine-readable data release (published each February via ScienceBase) ships the whole thing as normalized long-format CSV rather than PDF. Covers lithium, cobalt, rare earths, graphite, gallium, germanium, antimony — every critical mineral in the policy conversation.
- Docs: https://www.usgs.gov/centers/national-minerals-information-center/mineral-commodity-summaries
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no rate limit, US Government public domain. Publication cadence: one release per year (MCS 2026 published 2026-02-06). History: MCS series runs back to 1996 online, predecessor volumes to 1932. Mineral Industry Surveys give monthly/quarterly updates for selected commodities.
- Latency: annual (February) for MCS; monthly/quarterly for Mineral Industry Surveys | Format: CSV bulk via ScienceBase + PDF chapters
- Relevance: CORE for anything mineral-supply-shaped. It is the denominator everyone quotes: 'China controls X% of rare earth production' resolves against USGS. Prices contracts on country production share, reserve revisions, import-reliance thresholds, and critical-minerals-list membership. Annual cadence means it sets the baseline, not the tick.

**NYISO Public Market Data Files** — New York Independent System Operator `LIVE`

- Completely open CSV market data with no key at all: day-ahead and real-time zonal and generator-node LBMP with marginal loss and congestion components broken out, load forecasts, actual load, fuel mix, outage schedules, ancillary service prices, and transmission constraints. Files are date-addressed so you can backfill by URL construction.
- Docs: https://www.nyiso.com/custom-reports
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, no published rate limit. One CSV per day per report (e.g. /public/csv/damlbmp/YYYYMMDDdamlbmp_zone.csv), monthly ZIP archives for bulk backfill. History goes back to market inception (1999) for core price reports. Confirmed serving 2026-09-19 DAM zonal LBMP.
- Latency: 5-minute (real-time LBMP); day-ahead posted ~11:00 ET previous day | Format: CSV bulk (date-addressed static files) + monthly ZIP
- Relevance: CORE for US Northeast power contracts and the easiest ISO to integrate — no auth, no quota, trivially backfillable. Prices day-ahead peak price thresholds, congestion events, and NYC zone scarcity. The clean URL scheme makes it the best ISO to prototype your historical-error model against.

**CAISO OASIS** — California Independent System Operator `LIVE`

- Day-ahead, fifteen-minute and real-time five-minute LMP by pricing node, system load and forecasts, renewable curtailment, transmission outages, ancillary service requirements and prices, and the interconnection queue. Also the Today's Outlook feeds for fuel mix and net demand (the duck curve) at 5-minute resolution.
- Docs: https://www.caiso.com/library/technical-documentation
- Auth: none for OASIS SingleZip; registration only for some restricted reports | Limits: No API key required. CAISO enforces an undocumented per-IP throttle and a query-window cap — most queryname reports accept a maximum 31-day range per request and will reject longer windows. Exact requests-per-minute ceiling is not published: UNKNOWN. History back to 2009 for LMP.
- Latency: 5-minute (RTM LMP and fuel mix); day-ahead ~13:00 PT | Format: REST returning ZIP of CSV or XML (SingleZip endpoint)
- Relevance: CORE for California power and for solar/storage contracts generally. CAISO is where negative prices, curtailment records and battery-dispatch records happen first, so it prices duck-curve, curtailment-volume and negative-price-hour contracts. The nodal granularity also supports very specific location-based contracts.

**ERCOT Public Dashboards + MIS Reports** — Electric Reliability Council of Texas `LIVE`

- Unauthenticated JSON dashboard feeds for real-time fuel mix (with monthly installed capacity by fuel), system-wide demand and forecast, supply/demand reserve margin, wind and solar output and forecast, and real-time settlement point prices. The broader MIS report library adds nodal LMP, outages and 60-day disclosure data.
- Docs: https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo
- Auth: none for the dashboard JSON endpoints; free registration (ERCOT API Explorer / Public API) required for the full MIS product set | Limits: Dashboard JSON endpoints: no key, no published rate limit (UNKNOWN); each returns a rolling ~2-day window. The registered Public API has per-subscription quotas that ERCOT does not publish publicly: UNKNOWN. Deep history requires the MIS archive, not the dashboards.
- Latency: 5-minute (fuel mix, prices, reserve margin) | Format: REST JSON (dashboards) + CSV/ZIP (MIS)
- Relevance: CORE — ERCOT is the highest-variance grid in the developed world and therefore the most heavily traded in prediction markets. Prices summer/winter peak demand records, scarcity pricing events, reserve margin EEA declarations, and rolling blackout contracts. Confirmed serving live 2026-09-20 data with full capacity-by-fuel breakdown.

**PJM Data Miner 2** — PJM Interconnection `LIVE`

- The largest US grid operator (65 million people). Day-ahead and real-time hourly and five-minute nodal LMP, load and forecasts, fuel mix, generation outages, capacity auction (RPM) results, interconnection queue, and ancillary services — several hundred datasets.
- Docs: https://dataminer2.pjm.com/
- Auth: free registration required — Data Miner 2 account issues an Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key for api.pjm.com | Limits: Free tier confirmed to exist (api.pjm.com returns 401 without a subscription key). PJM applies per-subscription rate limits and a rows-per-request cap that it does not publish on the public docs page: UNKNOWN. Bulk historical download is supported through the web UI with row caps per export. History back to 1998 for core LMP series.
- Latency: 5-minute (RT LMP); day-ahead posted afternoon prior | Format: REST JSON (api.pjm.com, subscription key header) + CSV export
- Relevance: CORE by sheer size — PJM prices set the Eastern Interconnection tone, and its capacity auction results have repeatedly been prediction-market events in their own right. Gate on getting the free subscription key early; it is the one CORE US ISO with a registration wall.

**JODI Oil and Gas World Database** — Joint Organisations Data Initiative (IEA/OPEC/UN/Eurostat/APEC/GECF/OLADE) `LIVE`

- Monthly national submissions of oil production, refinery intake and output, imports, exports, closing stocks and demand by product (crude, LPG, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil), plus the JODI-Gas equivalent for natural gas production, imports, exports, stocks and demand. Roughly 100 reporting countries including most OPEC members.
- Docs: https://www.jodidata.org/oil/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration. Full world database as a single CSV inside a ZIP (world_primary_csv.zip), confirmed downloadable. History from 2002 for oil, 2009 for gas. No API — bulk file only, republished monthly.
- Latency: monthly, with roughly a 2-month reporting lag; individual countries sometimes lag further or revise | Format: CSV bulk (ZIP)
- Relevance: CORE for non-US oil supply, and the only free source of self-reported OPEC-member production and stock data. Prices OPEC compliance contracts, Saudi/Iraq/UAE output-level contracts, and global inventory-draw narratives. Caveat that matters: JODI is self-reported and unevenly revised — a missing country-month is a missing measurement, not a zero, and treating it as zero will silently corrupt any aggregate you compute.

**UN Comtrade (public preview + full API)** — United Nations Statistics Division `LIVE`

- Bilateral trade flows by HS commodity code, reporter, partner, year or month, in both value and physical quantity. Every commodity in this domain has a code: 2709 crude, 2711 gas/LNG, 2701 coal, 2601 iron ore, 2603 copper ore, 2605 cobalt ore, 2530.90/2805.30 rare earths, 2844 uranium, 2836.91 lithium carbonate.
- Docs: https://comtradedeveloper.un.org/
- Auth: public preview endpoint needs no key; the full data API needs a free subscription key (registration) | Limits: Public preview (comtradeapi.un.org/public/v1/preview/...): no key, capped at 500 records per call, confirmed responding. Free registered tier: 500 calls per day with a 250,000-record daily allowance and 100 records per call by default. Annual data from 1962, monthly from 2010. Premium tiers raise both.
- Latency: monthly (typically 2-4 month lag, longer for some reporters) | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: CORE for the export-ban and resource-nationalism question the user specifically asked about. When Indonesia bans nickel ore or the DRC quotas cobalt, Comtrade is where you measure whether the ban is actually binding on physical flows rather than rhetorical. Slow, but it is ground truth on trade.

**EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (direct files)** — US Energy Information Administration `LIVE`

- The single most market-moving recurring energy release in the world, as direct files: crude oil stocks including Cushing, gasoline and distillate stocks, refinery inputs and utilization rate, crude production estimate, SPR level, and imports — all by PADD. Served as psw01.xls and the dnav historical series files (e.g. WCESTUS1w.xls for weekly crude ending stocks) independently of the API.
- Docs: https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/
- Auth: none for the direct file paths | Limits: No key, no rate limit on the static file paths. Weekly history for core stock series runs back to 1982 in the dnav XLS files. Note: ir.eia.gov/wpsr/wpsrsummary.csv returned 403 to a scripted fetch while ir.eia.gov/wpsr/psw01.xls returned 200 — use the XLS paths, and prefer the API v2 route for anything automated.
- Latency: weekly — Wednesday 10:30 ET (Thursday when Monday is a holiday) | Format: XLS bulk (static files)
- Relevance: CORE. Crude-build-vs-draw contracts resolve on this exact print, and the Wednesday 10:30 release is a scheduled volatility event you can build a whole market-timing layer around. Having the direct file as well as the API gives you a second path when the API throttles at release time — which is precisely when everyone hits it.

**NRC Power Reactor Status Reports** — US Nuclear Regulatory Commission

- Daily percent-of-full-power for every operating US commercial reactor, with a reason code and narrative when a unit is below 100% (refueling outage, forced shutdown, coastdown, turbine trip, grid-related reduction). Published as individual daily pages plus a rolling 365-day raw text file and an Excel data dictionary.
- Docs: https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/event-status/reactor-status/index
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, US Government public domain. Rolling raw text file covers the last 365 days; yearly index pages archive further back (per-year directories exist from the late 1990s). Data collected between 04:00 and 08:00 ET daily, all times Eastern. NOTE: nrc.gov returned HTTP 403 to both curl and an automated fetcher — it bot-blocks non-browser user agents, so a scraper needs realistic headers or a headless browser. I confirmed the 2026 pages exist via search but did NOT successfully fetch the file myself.
- Latency: daily (morning) | Format: TXT bulk (365-day raw file) + HTML daily pages + XLSX dictionary
- Relevance: CORE for nuclear and underrated for power generally. A reactor dropping from 100% to 0% overnight is ~1 GW off a grid, and this file reports it before most commercial terminals surface it. Prices reactor-restart-date, capacity-factor and outage-duration contracts, and feeds regional supply models directly.

**Baker Hughes Rig Count** — Baker Hughes

- The industry-standard weekly count of active drilling rigs: US total split oil/gas/miscellaneous and by basin (Permian, Eagle Ford, Williston, Marcellus…), directional/horizontal/vertical split, Canada, and an international monthly count by country. History to 1944 for the US count.
- Docs: https://rigcount.bakerhughes.com/
- Auth: none stated | Limits: Published as downloadable spreadsheets on the rig count site; no key and no stated quota. NOTE: rigcount.bakerhughes.com returned a connection timeout and then HTTP 403 to automated fetches — it is behind bot protection, so the exact current file URLs and any caps are UNKNOWN to me. I did not confirm the download path. Third-party mirrors (YCharts, Barchart cmdty, AOGR) carry the series but most gate history behind paid tiers.
- Latency: weekly — released noon Central Time on the last working day of the week (normally Friday); international count monthly | Format: XLSX bulk (site download), scrape-only in practice given the bot wall
- Relevance: CORE as a leading indicator of US shale supply 4-6 months forward, and there are direct rig-count-threshold contracts. Budget real effort for acquisition though — this is a headline number with a scraping problem, and the free API wrappers that claim to serve it are mostly reselling it behind their own paywalls.

**Global Energy Monitor Trackers** — Global Energy Monitor (non-profit) `LIVE`

- Asset-level global registers maintained by researchers: Global Coal Mine Tracker (every mine over a size threshold with capacity, status, owner, coordinates, opening/closing dates), Global Coal Plant Tracker, Global Oil & Gas Extraction Tracker, Integrated Power Tracker, LNG Terminal Tracker, Steel Plant Tracker, and Iron Ore Mine Tracker. Genuinely global, which is exactly where USGS and MSHA stop.
- Docs: https://globalenergymonitor.org/projects/global-coal-mine-tracker/download-data/
- Auth: free download but gated behind a registration form (name/email/affiliation) per tracker | Limits: Free for non-commercial use under a CC BY licence; commercial use terms differ per tracker — read them before building a paid product on it. No API at all: XLSX bulk downloads only, refreshed on a roughly semi-annual release cycle per tracker. Exact per-download limits: none stated. History: status snapshots per release, not a continuous time series.
- Latency: semi-annual to annual releases | Format: XLSX bulk (registration-gated), no API
- Relevance: CORE for the mines-and-minerals question the user asked, precisely because it is the only free global asset-level register of mines and their capacities. It is the entity layer: it turns 'a mine in Indonesia halted' into 'X million tonnes per year of capacity at a named asset owned by a named company'. Slow cadence means it is a reference table, not a feed — pair it with a news feed for events.

**GDELT 2.0 (DOC API + 15-minute raw files)** — The GDELT Project `LIVE`

- Every news article the project can reach worldwide, in 100+ languages, with extracted themes, entities, locations, tone and images, updated every 15 minutes. The events and mentions tables are CAMEO-coded. This is the closest free thing to the 'god's eye' the user described, and for this domain it is the event layer over mines, refineries, pipelines, strikes, export bans and force majeure declarations.
- Docs: https://www.gdeltproject.org/data.html
- Auth: none | Limits: No key. DOC 2.0 API: the operator asks for no more than one request every 5 seconds — I hit this and got the throttle notice back, which confirms it is enforced. DOC API returns a maximum 250 articles per query and covers a rolling ~3-month window. Unrestricted deep history comes from the raw 15-minute CSV files at data.gdeltproject.org (v2 from Feb 2015, v1 events from 1979) with no quota at all, and from the BigQuery mirror (billed by Google, free tier only up to the monthly query allowance).
- Latency: 15-minute | Format: REST JSON (DOC API) + CSV bulk (ZIP per 15 minutes) + BigQuery
- Relevance: CORE as the event trigger across this entire domain. There is no structured feed for 'strike at Escondida' or 'Chile declares force majeure' — there is only news, and GDELT is the only free way to ingest news globally at minute resolution with entity and location extraction already done. Use the raw files for backfill and the DOC API only for interactive queries; the 5-second limit makes DOC unusable as a bulk path.

#### USEFUL

**USGS Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS) + MRData services** — USGS Mineral Resources Program `LIVE`

- Site-level database of over 300,000 mineral deposits and occurrences worldwide: coordinates, commodity list, deposit type, development status (producer, past producer, prospect, occurrence), host geology, ore control, production notes, and literature references. Plus companion layers — active mines and processing plants, geochemistry, geophysics, and the Global Mineral Resource Assessment.
- Docs: https://mrdata.usgs.gov/mrds/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no documented rate limit. Full CSV dump available at mrdata.usgs.gov/mrds/mrds-csv.zip. Also served as OGC WFS/WMS (GetCapabilities confirmed responding) for spatial queries. Static snapshot — MRDS itself is no longer actively maintained as a live register, so treat records as historical inventory not current status.
- Latency: static/irregular (legacy database, periodic republication) | Format: CSV bulk + OGC WFS/WMS + web query
- Relevance: USEFUL as the spatial join key. It turns a news headline ('explosion at a mine in Katanga') into structured context — which commodity, which deposit type, who else is nearby. Not a price feed; it is the entity resolution layer that makes mine-incident feeds machine-usable.

**World Bank Commodity Price Data (Pink Sheet) + Indicators API** — World Bank `LIVE`

- Monthly and annual nominal and real price series for 70+ commodities in one spreadsheet: crude (Brent, Dubai, WTI average), natural gas (US, Europe, Japan LNG), coal (Australian, South African), all major metals (aluminium, copper, iron ore, lead, nickel, tin, zinc), precious metals, fertilizers, and agriculture. Plus the Indicators REST API for country-level energy and mineral rents, energy use, and electricity access.
- Docs: https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/commodity-markets
- Auth: none | Limits: No key for either surface. Pink Sheet monthly historical XLSX confirmed downloadable; history from 1960 for most series. Indicators API (api.worldbank.org/v2/) has no published hard quota — be polite, paginate with per_page (max 32,500 per page).
- Latency: monthly (Pink Sheet, first days of month); annual for most Indicators series | Format: XLSX bulk (Pink Sheet) + REST JSON/XML (Indicators)
- Relevance: USEFUL as the neutral cross-commodity reference. Its value is the 1960-present consistent methodology across 70 commodities — ideal for base rates and cross-commodity correlation, too slow for tick-level pricing. Settles monthly-average-price contracts.

**CFTC Commitments of Traders (COT)** — US Commodity Futures Trading Commission `LIVE`

- Weekly speculative and commercial positioning for every US futures market — crude, natural gas, gasoline, heating oil, gold, silver, copper, platinum, palladium — broken into producer/merchant, swap dealer, managed money and other reportable, long/short/spreading, plus open interest and number of traders. Available as fixed-width text and as a full Socrata JSON/SoQL API.
- Docs: https://publicreporting.cftc.gov/
- Auth: none (optional free Socrata app token raises throughput) | Limits: Socrata without an app token: shared anonymous pool, throttled per IP — exact anonymous limit not published by CFTC (UNKNOWN); with a free app token limits are per-token and far higher. SoQL $limit defaults to 1,000, max 50,000 per request with $offset paging. History in the Socrata disaggregated dataset goes back to 2006; legacy text archives to 1986.
- Latency: weekly — positions as of Tuesday close, published Friday 15:30 ET | Format: REST JSON (Socrata SoQL) + fixed-width TXT
- Relevance: USEFUL and distinctly non-obvious. It does not predict price directly, but extreme managed-money positioning is the single best free indicator of how crowded a commodity trade is — which is exactly what tells you whether a prediction market's implied probability is being set by conviction or by positioning. Also settles COT-specific contracts.

**MISO Real-Time Data Broker** — Midcontinent Independent System Operator `LIVE`

- Unauthenticated JSON/XML feeds for real-time fuel mix, total load and forecast, wind and solar generation and forecast, regional directional transfer limits, and consolidated LMP across the MISO footprint (15 US states plus Manitoba).
- Docs: https://www.misoenergy.org/markets-and-operations/real-time--market-data/market-reports/
- Auth: none for the DataBrokerServices endpoints | Limits: No key required. No published rate limit: UNKNOWN. Data Broker serves current/rolling values only — historical backfill must come from the Market Reports archive (daily CSV/XLS files, addressable by date, back several years).
- Latency: 5-minute | Format: REST JSON/XML (DataBrokerServices.asmx) + CSV/XLS market reports
- Relevance: USEFUL. MISO matters for Midwest winter reliability contracts and for coal-vs-gas dispatch share, and it is the footprint where capacity auction shortfalls have repeatedly surprised. Lower contract volume than ERCOT or CAISO, so rank it below them.

**Grid Status API (gridstatus.io)** — Grid Status (commercial, with free tier) `LIVE`

- One normalized schema across CAISO, SPP, ISO-NE, MISO, ERCOT, NYISO, PJM, IESO, AESO and EIA. Hundreds of curated datasets — day-ahead and real-time LMP and settlement point prices, load and load forecasts, fuel mix, storage, ancillary prices, interconnection queues — with the per-ISO format chaos already solved.
- Docs: https://docs.gridstatus.io/developers/api-reference/api-usage
- Auth: free API key (self-service signup); key required — unauthenticated requests return 401 | Limits: Free tier exists and is key-gated. Third-party sources cite 500,000 rows returned per month on the free tier, but I could NOT confirm that number on the official pricing or docs page (both returned 403 to programmatic fetch), so treat it as UNKNOWN until you read it in-account. The API response itself exposes the live values in fields api_rows_returned_limit, api_requests_limit, api_rows_per_response_limit, per_second/per_minute/per_hour_api_rate_limit — read your own limits from a live call rather than trusting any published figure. Some premium endpoints and deep history are paid-only.
- Latency: 5-minute to hourly, matching the upstream ISO | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: USEFUL — high leverage for build speed, but do not make it structural. Pulling seven ISOs through one schema saves weeks, yet the free row budget will not survive a Bloomberg-terminal-grade backfill and it is a single commercial dependency in front of data you can get direct and free. Use it to prototype, then migrate the CORE ISOs to their own feeds.

**UK Carbon Intensity API** — National Grid ESO / NESO `LIVE`

- Half-hourly actual and forecast carbon intensity for Great Britain, national and by 14 regions and by postcode, plus the generation mix percentage by fuel (gas, coal, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro, biomass, imports) behind each reading. Forecasts extend 48 hours ahead.
- Docs: https://carbon-intensity.github.io/api-definitions/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, no published rate limit (the maintainers ask for reasonable use). History from 2017 via /intensity/{from}/{to} with a 14-day maximum window per request. Confirmed returning live 2026-09-20 forecast=125 / actual=140 gCO2/kWh.
- Latency: half-hourly, with 48-hour forecast | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: USEFUL. The forecast-vs-actual pair is the interesting part — it is a free, continuously published, publicly auditable forecast with known error, which is exactly the shape of a model-vs-market comparison. Prices GB coal-free-record and wind-record contracts.

**NESO Data Portal (CKAN)** — National Energy System Operator (Great Britain) `LIVE`

- Several hundred GB grid datasets over a standard CKAN API: 1/2/7/14-day-ahead demand and wind forecasts, 24-month-ahead constraint cost forecasts and constraint limits, balancing services adjustment data, historic generation mix, embedded solar and wind estimates, day-ahead constraint flows, and interconnector flows. Package list confirmed returning live.
- Docs: https://www.neso.energy/data-portal
- Auth: none | Limits: No key. Standard CKAN action API (package_list, package_show, datastore_search, datastore_search_sql). datastore_search default limit 100, max 32,000 rows per request with offset paging. No published request-per-minute cap: UNKNOWN. History varies per dataset, many back to 2009-2015.
- Latency: varies — half-hourly for operational series, daily for forecasts | Format: REST JSON (CKAN) + CSV resources
- Relevance: USEFUL for GB power. NOTE: the old api.nationalgrideso.com host is DEAD — it no longer resolves. Anything pointing at that hostname (including several GitHub wrappers and blog tutorials) is stale; use api.neso.energy.

**Energi Data Service** — Energinet (Danish TSO) `LIVE`

- Nordic and German power market data with no key whatsoever: Elspot prices by price area (DK1, DK2, DE, NO, SE areas) in DKK and EUR, production and consumption by type, CO2 emissions, gas system data, balancing prices, and electricity import/export.
- Docs: https://www.energidataservice.dk/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, no published rate limit (UNKNOWN). Query with limit/offset/start/end/filter/sort; default limit 100. History for Elspotprices runs back to 2014. Confirmed returning live records.
- Latency: hourly (spot prices published day-ahead ~13:00 CET) | Format: REST JSON (also CSV, XLSX)
- Relevance: USEFUL. The genuinely valuable property is that it carries German (DE) spot prices with zero auth — Germany is the EU power benchmark and the usual route to it (ENTSO-E) needs a token with a 3-day wait. Good day-one integration and a good cross-check on ENTSO-E.

**Energy-Charts API** — Fraunhofer ISE `LIVE`

- Quarter-hourly public power generation by source, installed capacity, day-ahead prices by bidding zone, cross-border flows, and emission factors for Germany and most European countries. Clean numeric arrays keyed by unix timestamps.
- Docs: https://api.energy-charts.info/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration. No published rate limit: UNKNOWN (Fraunhofer asks for fair use and caching). History back to 2015 for German series, varying for other countries. Confirmed returning live 2026-09 quarter-hourly data.
- Latency: 15-minute | Format: REST JSON (OpenAPI documented)
- Relevance: USEFUL. The best no-auth path to European generation mix and prices, and quarter-hourly resolution beats ENTSO-E's hourly for intraday work. Prices German renewable-share records, negative-price-hour counts and coal-dispatch contracts.

**Ember Electricity Data API** — Ember (energy think tank, non-profit) `LIVE`

- Harmonized global electricity data — monthly and yearly generation by fuel, demand, installed capacity, power sector emissions and carbon intensity — for essentially every country, on one consistent methodology. This is the dataset most 'X country hit Y% renewables' headlines are computed from.
- Docs: https://api.ember-energy.org/v1/docs
- Auth: free API key requested from ember-energy.org/data/api | Limits: Free API key, no charge. Ember does not publish numeric rate limits — enforcement is per-key and signalled by HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Exact calls/day: UNKNOWN. Monthly data typically lags ~2 months; yearly series run back to 2000 for most countries.
- Latency: monthly (with ~2-month lag); yearly | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: USEFUL for the global cross-country contracts that EIA and ENTSO-E do not reach — 'will India's coal share fall below X', 'will global solar exceed Y TWh'. Too slow for anything intraday, authoritative for annual and monthly milestone contracts. NOTE: the older api.ember-climate.org domain is superseded by api.ember-energy.org.

**US Census International Trade API** — US Census Bureau `LIVE`

- Monthly US imports and exports by HS code down to 10 digits, by country, district and port, in value and quantity. Far faster than Comtrade for the US leg, and includes petroleum, LNG, coal, and every critical-mineral HS line.
- Docs: https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/international-trade.html
- Auth: free API key (self-service); small numbers of calls work keyless | Limits: Without a key: limited to 500 queries per IP per day. With a free key: no published hard cap, but Census throttles abusive patterns (exact ceiling UNKNOWN). Monthly series from 2013 in the API; earlier via USA Trade Online. Data released ~35 days after month end.
- Latency: monthly, ~5 weeks after month end | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: USEFUL. The fastest official read on US LNG export volumes, crude export destinations, and US dependence on specific critical-mineral import sources. Prices US-LNG-export-record and import-reliance contracts. Complements Comtrade rather than duplicating it — Census is faster, Comtrade is global.

**MSHA Open Government Data** — US Mine Safety and Health Administration `LIVE`

- Mine-level US data: the full mine register with operator, commodity, status (active, abandoned, temporarily idled) and employment; quarterly production by mine; every reportable accident, injury and fatality with narrative; inspections, violations, citations and civil penalties; and closure orders. Accidents.zip confirmed downloadable.
- Docs: https://www.msha.gov/data-and-reports/mine-data-retrieval-system
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, US Government public domain. Full-table ZIP/TXT extracts with data definition files; no request quota. History: accident and violation files run back to 1983, production data back to the 1990s. Refreshed roughly weekly.
- Latency: weekly refresh of bulk files; quarterly for production | Format: CSV/TXT bulk (ZIP)
- Relevance: USEFUL and the closest thing to a real mine-incident feed that exists as structured open data — but US-only, which is its hard limit. It will tell you when a US coal or copper mine takes a closure order; it will tell you nothing about Katanga, Chile or Indonesia. Prices US coal production and mine-safety contracts; use it as the template for what you wish existed globally.

**FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data)** — Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis `LIVE`

- Hundreds of thousands of series including daily WTI and Brent spot (DCOILWTICO, DCOILBRENTEU), Henry Hub gas, PPI series for metal ores, coal and petroleum, industrial production indices for mining, global price indices for copper/aluminium/nickel/iron ore, and US energy CPI components. Many series are FRED's mirror of EIA, World Bank and IMF data with a single uniform interface and vintage history.
- Docs: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/fred/
- Auth: free API key (self-service registration) | Limits: Free key required — keyless requests return an explicit 400 'Variable api_key is not set', which confirms the service is live. FRED does not publish a numeric hard cap; it applies per-key throttling and returns 429 on abuse. Exact calls/minute: UNKNOWN (community consensus is roughly 120/minute, not officially documented). Up to 100,000 observations per request. ALFRED gives real-time vintages so you can see what a number was before revision.
- Latency: daily for oil/gas price series; monthly for PPI and production indices | Format: REST JSON/XML
- Relevance: USEFUL as the convenience layer and the revision layer. The vintage (ALFRED) feature is the non-obvious value: if a contract resolves on an as-first-published number, FRED is the only free place to recover what was actually printed before revision — which is a resolution-dispute problem nobody thinks about until it bites.

**Sodir FactPages (Norwegian Offshore Directorate)** — Sodir / Norwegian Offshore Directorate `LIVE`

- Field-by-field monthly production of oil, gas, NGL and condensate for every Norwegian field, plus wellbore data, licence ownership, discovery history, reserves estimates and facility status. Norway is Europe's swing gas supplier, so this is the field-level ground truth behind European gas balance.
- Docs: https://factpages.sodir.no/en/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration. Table views export as CSV/XLSX directly by URL, and there is a documented set of downloadable tables. No published rate limit: UNKNOWN. Monthly field production history runs from the 1970s.
- Latency: monthly (production figures published around the 20th for the prior month) | Format: CSV/XLSX bulk via tableview URLs
- Relevance: USEFUL for European gas contracts specifically. Norwegian field outages and maintenance are a recurring driver of TTF spikes, and this is the primary source rather than a commentary layer. Analogous free registers exist for the UK (NSTA) and Brazil (ANP) if you want the same shape for other basins.

#### NICHE

**Electricity Maps API** — Electricity Maps (commercial, with free tier) `LIVE`

- Real-time, historical and 24-72h forecast carbon intensity and power breakdown by source for 200+ zones worldwide, plus import/export flows between zones. The /v3/zones endpoint listing all zones is fully open.
- Docs: https://portal.electricitymaps.com/docs/api
- Auth: free API key for the free tier (zone chosen at signup); /v3/zones is open with no key | Limits: Free tier: 50 requests per hour, and restricted to ONE zone chosen at account creation. Hourly resolution. Historical range and forecast access on the free tier are limited — full history and multi-zone access are paid. The 50/hour and one-zone figures come from the vendor help centre, not from a page I fetched directly.
- Latency: hourly | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: NICHE for prediction markets specifically. Carbon intensity contracts are rare, and the one-zone free cap kills breadth. Its genuine use is as an independent cross-check on a single high-value zone's fuel mix. Do not build the grid layer on this — build it on EIA-930 and ENTSO-E.

**ESIOS API** — Red Eléctrica de España (Spanish TSO) `LIVE`

- ~2,000 indicators for the Spanish and Iberian power system: demand real/forecast/scheduled, generation by technology, PVPC retail prices, day-ahead and intraday market prices, interconnection flows with France/Portugal/Morocco, CO2 intensity, and reserve/restriction market results.
- Docs: https://api.esios.ree.es/
- Auth: free personal token by emailing consultasios@ree.es | Limits: Token required for indicator data; the /indicators catalogue responds without one. No published request-per-minute cap: UNKNOWN. Query windows are per-indicator; history for core demand and price indicators runs back to 2014.
- Latency: 10-minute to hourly depending on indicator | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: NICHE for global prediction markets, but genuinely CORE if Iberian power or the Iberian exception mechanism is in scope. Spain is also the cleanest natural experiment in high-solar-penetration price collapse, which makes it good model-fitting data even if you never trade it.

**Open Power System Data** — OPSD consortium (Neon, DIW Berlin, TU Berlin et al.) `LIVE`

- Curated, versioned, research-grade European power datasets: hourly time series of load, wind and solar generation and capacity by country and control area; a conventional power plant register for Germany and neighbours; national generation capacity; and household data. Every package is versioned with a datapackage.json and full provenance.
- Docs: https://data.open-power-system-data.org/
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, open licence. Full CSV/SQLite/XLSX bulk downloads. NOTE: OPSD is a completed research project — packages are versioned snapshots and the time series stop at their last release rather than updating live. History is deep and clean; currency is not there.
- Latency: static versioned releases (project concluded — not a live feed) | Format: CSV / SQLite / XLSX bulk with datapackage metadata
- Relevance: NICHE for live pricing, USEFUL for model fitting. Treat it as a clean, documented historical training corpus for European power, not as a feed. If you need current EU data, use ENTSO-E or energy-charts; if you need ten clean years to fit an error model, this is better prepared than anything you would assemble yourself.

#### Repos

- `gridstatus/gridstatus` — Python library that pulls data directly from CAISO, SPP, ISO-NE, MISO, ERCOT, NYISO, PJM, IESO, AESO and EIA and normalizes it into pandas DataFrames — fuel mix, load, load forecasts, day-ahead and real-time LMP, storage, ancillary prices, interconnection queues. · The single highest-leverage repo in this domain. It solves the per-ISO format chaos that would otherwise eat weeks, and it works against the free public endpoints directly — you do not need the paid gridstatus.io API to use the library. Steal its per-ISO parsers even if you write your own ingestion.
- `EnergieID/entsoe-py` — Mature Python client for the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform that handles the XML schema, document type codes, bidding zone mappings and pagination, returning pandas objects. · ENTSO-E's raw API is XML with opaque document-type codes (A65, A75, A80…) and area EIC codes. This library encodes all of that mapping. Writing it yourself is a multi-day exercise in reading a PDF spec; the outage endpoints in particular are painful to parse by hand.
- `electricitymaps/electricitymaps-contrib` — The open-source parser collection behind the Electricity Maps app — per-country/per-zone scrapers for grid generation mix and flows covering 200+ zones, plus the zone configuration and capacity data. · This is the real prize, not the Electricity Maps API. The parsers are open and they target each country's own TSO endpoint directly, so you can bypass the 50-requests-per-hour one-zone free tier entirely and hit the upstream sources yourself. It is effectively a crowdsourced map of every national grid data source on earth.
- `Arpeggeo/awesome-mining-data` — Curated list of open mining-industry datasets: drillhole, geochemistry, geophysics and block model data from Queensland, Western Australia (WAEGO, WACHEM), South Australia (SARIG), Ireland (Lisheen, Galmoy), Yukon (Macpass), plus synthetic benchmarks and mineral reference databases. · The best single index of geological/exploration open data, a layer USGS does not cover well outside the US. Caveat worth knowing up front: almost none of these expose a programmatic API — they are portal downloads and map viewers, so plan for bulk ingestion rather than polling.
- `GlobalEnergyMonitor` — GitHub organization for Global Energy Monitor, publishing tooling and supporting code around their asset-level trackers (coal mines, coal plants, oil & gas extraction, LNG terminals, steel plants, iron ore mines). · The trackers themselves are registration-gated XLSX, but the org's repos give you schema documentation, ID conventions and processing code — which is what you need to join their asset register against USGS MRDS, MSHA and news entity extraction. Asset ID reconciliation is the hard part of this domain and this is where the conventions are documented.
- `DARPA-CRITICALMAAS/ta2-extraction` — DARPA CriticalMAAS program code for extracting structured mineral resource information — deposit types, mineral inventory, grades, tonnages, site locations and report references — out of unstructured mining documents and technical reports. · Directly relevant to the hardest problem in this domain: NI 43-101 and JORC technical reports contain the real reserve and production-guidance numbers and they are PDFs. This is government-funded extraction tooling for exactly that. If you want mineral reserves as structured data rather than headlines, start here.
- `truptimohanty/mineral-ai` — Ingests ten years of USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries and serves a RAG interface over reserves, production, market share, usage and price for ~90 commodities. · A working reference implementation of the USGS MCS parsing pipeline — the chapter PDFs and data-release CSVs have awkward, inconsistent structure across years. Worth reading for the normalization logic even if you discard the RAG layer, which is the least interesting part.
- `ember-energy/ember-data-api` — Source for Ember's own data API serving their harmonized global electricity generation, demand, capacity and emissions datasets. · Documents the schema and the country/fuel harmonization decisions behind the numbers. Since Ember's series is what most global electricity headlines are computed from, knowing exactly how they classify fuels matters when a contract turns on a definitional boundary like 'clean' versus 'renewable'.
- `alex9smith/gdelt-doc-api` — Python wrapper for the GDELT DOC 2.0 API with filter construction for keywords, themes, domains, languages, countries and date ranges, returning article lists and timeline volume series. · Makes GDELT's query syntax tractable and handles the timeline modes that are genuinely useful for event detection — article volume spikes around a commodity keyword are a usable early signal. Pair with linwoodc3/gdeltPyR for the raw 15-minute event files, since the DOC API's 5-second rate limit and 3-month window make it unusable for backfill.
- `PyPSA/pypsa-eur` — Open optimization model of the European transmission system with a full automated data pipeline that pulls ENTSO-E, OPSD, Copernicus weather, and OpenStreetMap network data into a consistent network representation. · Its Snakemake data-retrieval rules are a working, maintained inventory of which European energy datasets are actually fetchable and how — effectively a tested manifest of live EU energy data URLs. Even if you never run the optimization, the retrieval layer saves you rediscovering dead endpoints.
- `linwoodc3/gdeltPyR` — Python library for pulling and parsing GDELT v1 and v2 raw event, mention and GKG files into pandas, handling the 15-minute file naming, CAMEO code decoding and column schemas. · The raw GDELT files are the unrestricted path — no rate limit, history to 1979 — but the schemas are undocumented positional CSV with ~60 columns. This library encodes them. It is the difference between GDELT being usable for backfill and not.
- `ranaroussi/yfinance` — Python interface to Yahoo Finance data, covering commodity futures continuous contracts (CL=F crude, NG=F gas, GC=F gold, HG=F copper, SI=F silver), mining equities, and commodity ETFs with intraday and long daily history. · Pragmatic gap-filler for futures prices, which are otherwise the most paywalled part of this domain — CME, LME and ICE all bot-block or charge. Be honest about what it is: an unofficial scrape of an undocumented endpoint with no SLA and no terms permitting redistribution. Fine for research and model fitting, unsafe as the resolution source for a contract.

---

### Politics, Elections and Government (US + international) — free data feeds, verified September 2026

#### CORE

**openFEC API (v1)** — US Federal Election Commission `LIVE`

- Candidates, committees, filings, itemized receipts and disbursements, independent expenditures, electioneering communications, Schedule A/B/E line items, candidate totals by cycle, filing footnotes. Also FEC-certified federal election results. Itemized individual contributions go back to 1975; candidate/committee summaries from 1979. Nightly-to-intraday refresh as filings post (electronic filings appear within ~hours; paper Senate filings lag).
- Docs: https://api.open.fec.gov/developers/
- Base: `https://api.open.fec.gov/v1/`
- Auth: free API key (api.data.gov signup); DEMO_KEY works for testing | Limits: 1,000 requests/hour per registered key — this is the api.data.gov shared default, confirmed verbatim in the api.data.gov developer manual ('Hourly Limit: 1,000 requests per hour'), applied across ALL api.data.gov services on that one key. DEMO_KEY measured live: x-ratelimit-limit: 10 (per hour). Any FEC-specific per-minute sub-cap: UNKNOWN — not found in docs. Bulk flat files at fec.gov/data/browse-data/?tab=bulk-data are unmetered and are the correct path for full-cycle pulls. History depth: 1975+ itemized, 1979+ summaries.
- Latency: sub-daily (filing-driven); quarterly/monthly reporting cadence means real economic latency is weeks | Format: REST JSON (OpenAPI/Swagger) + CSV bulk
- Relevance: Prices 'will X run', 'who wins the primary', and candidate-viability contracts. Cash-on-hand and burn rate at the end-of-quarter filing is the single best public leading indicator of a primary drop-out contract. IE spending by outside groups is the best real-time read on which races the parties actually believe are competitive — far more honest than public messaging.

**Congress.gov API (v3)** — US Library of Congress `LIVE`

- Bills and resolutions (text, actions, cosponsors, committees, related bills, subjects), amendments, public laws, members, committees and reports, Congressional Record, House/Senate communications, treaties, and — critically — the /nomination endpoint covering presidential nominations and Senate confirmation status. Bills from the 93rd Congress (1973) forward for structured data; some collections deeper.
- Docs: https://github.com/LibraryOfCongress/api.congress.gov
- Base: `https://api.congress.gov/v3/`
- Auth: free API key (api.data.gov signup) | Limits: 5,000 requests/hour per key. This number comes from Library of Congress documentation/changelog (raised from 1,000/hour in March 2024) — I did NOT independently exhaust the limit to measure it, so treat 5,000 as documented-not-measured. DEMO_KEY measured live: x-ratelimit-limit: 10/hour. Returns HTTP 429 on exceed; rolling-hour window. Page size cap 250 per request. History depth: 93rd Congress (1973)+ for bills; members back to 1789 via bioguide linkage.
- Latency: hourly to daily (Congress.gov ingest cadence) | Format: REST JSON/XML
- Relevance: CORE for 'will bill X pass by date D', 'will nominee Y be confirmed', 'will the shutdown end by D' contracts. The /nomination endpoint plus action timestamps let you build an empirical base rate for cloture-to-confirmation lag, which is exactly the hazard function these contracts need. Bill action history gives you the survival curve for legislation by chamber and stage.

**Federal Register API (v1)** — US National Archives / GPO `LIVE`

- Every document published in the Federal Register: proposed rules, final rules, notices, and ALL presidential documents — executive orders, memoranda, proclamations, determinations. Full text, agency, docket IDs, effective dates, comment close dates, CFR citations, RIN, and links to the Regulations.gov docket. Also public inspection documents (published before the official FR issue — a genuine latency edge). Full text 1994-present; 1936-1993 available as scanned/bulk.
- Docs: https://www.federalregister.gov/developers/documentation/api/v1
- Base: `https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/`
- Auth: none — no API key required | Limits: No API key and NO published hard rate limit — exact calls/day and calls/minute: UNKNOWN (the docs state fair-use only). Measured live: a query for conditions[presidential_document_type][]=executive_order returned count=1564 with total_pages=50 at per_page=1, i.e. there is a server-side page cap; the response supplies a next_page_url carrying a search_after cursor, which is the supported path for deep pagination past that cap. Max per_page appears to be 1000 (documented, not measured). History depth: 1994+ full text.
- Latency: daily, with public-inspection documents appearing ~1 business day AHEAD of official publication | Format: REST JSON/CSV, plus bulk XML from GPO
- Relevance: The single best free feed for executive-action contracts: 'will Trump sign an EO on X by date D', 'will rule Y be finalized before the CRA window closes'. The public-inspection endpoint gives you sight of a document before it is officially published — measurable minutes-to-hours of edge on EO contracts. Effective-date and comment-close fields let you build a calendar of forced regulatory events.

**CourtListener REST API (v4) + Free Law Project bulk data** — Free Law Project `LIVE`

- Case law opinions and clusters (SCOTUS, federal circuits and districts, all 50 state appellate systems), PACER dockets/entries/documents/parties/attorneys via RECAP (~500M items), oral argument audio, judge biographical and appointment data, judicial financial disclosures, citation graph, and alerts/webhooks on docket activity. Opinions collection maintained since 2009 with much deeper historical backfill.
- Docs: https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/api/rest/v4/overview
- Base: `https://www.courtlistener.com/api/rest/v4/`
- Auth: free account token (HTTP Token auth) strongly recommended; some endpoints readable anonymously | Limits: EXACT, read verbatim from the v4 overview wiki and this is severe: authenticated users default to 5 requests per MINUTE, 50 per HOUR, and 125 per DAY. Rolling-window, all three throttles apply concurrently, most restrictive wins. Anonymous limits are not stated in the docs — UNKNOWN. Free Law Project membership expands access; commercial agreements exist. Because 125/day makes any polling strategy hopeless, the FREE BULK DATA DUMPS (https://www.courtlistener.com/help/api/bulk-data/) are the real integration path — download and query locally, use the API only for deltas and webhooks. History depth: SCOTUS to 1754, federal appellate deep, RECAP from 2009.
- Latency: near-real-time for docket alerts/webhooks; bulk dumps refresh periodically | Format: REST JSON + webhooks + CSV/bulk dumps
- Relevance: CORE for 'will SCOTUS rule on X by end of term', election-law and redistricting litigation contracts, ballot-access challenges, and any 'will the court enjoin policy Y' market. Docket webhooks are the fastest free signal that an opinion or injunction has landed. Judge appointment data supports panel-composition priors on circuit outcomes.

**Voteview bulk roll-call and DW-NOMINATE data** — UCLA / Voteview (Poole-Rosenthal-Lewis) `LIVE`

- Every recorded roll-call vote in the US House and Senate from 1789 to the present, as flat CSVs: member-level vote choices (HS###_votes.csv), roll-call metadata with outcome and vote counts (HS###_rollcalls.csv), and member ideal points (HS###_members.csv) with DW-NOMINATE dimension-1/2 coordinates, party, state, district, ICPSR and bioguide IDs. Current Congress is live — I fetched HS119_rollcalls.csv (464 KB) and HS119_members.csv (65 KB) successfully.
- Docs: https://voteview.com/data
- Base: `https://voteview.com/static/data/out/`
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no registration, no published rate limit — UNKNOWN exact cap; these are static CSVs on a CDN-style path, so practical limits are bandwidth-bound. File sizes measured: HS118_votes.csv = 16.5 MB. History depth: 1st Congress (1789) through the 119th (current), complete.
- Latency: periodic — updated in batches during a session, typically within days of votes | Format: CSV bulk (also DTA/Rdata); an unofficial JSON API exists but did not resolve in my test
- Relevance: CORE for 'will bill X get 60 votes', 'will member Y defect', 'will the motion to vacate succeed'. DW-NOMINATE ideal points plus the full historical vote matrix let you build a per-member defection probability conditioned on where a bill sits in ideological space — a genuinely calibrated vote-count model rather than pundit arithmetic. Also the base for whip-count contracts.

**Silver Bulletin pollster ratings + raw polls dataset (THE historical polling error source)** — Silver Bulletin / Nate Silver `LIVE`

- THE dataset that turns a poll into a probability. Two free XLSX downloads, January 2026 update: (1) 'Pollster Stats Full 2026' (measured 132,271 bytes) with per-pollster Predictive Plus-Minus, Simple Average Error, mean-reverted partisan bias, Advanced Plus-Minus, house effects, herding penalty, transparency/AAPOR status, and letter grade; (2) 'Rawpolls' (measured 2,048,058 bytes) — raw poll-level records for MORE THAN 12,300 POLLS back to 1998, each with the polled margin AND the actual certified result, i.e. the signed error per poll, per race, per state, per pollster. Continues the Nate-era FiveThirtyEight methodology unbroken across the 538 shutdown.
- Docs: https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin
- Base: `https://www.natesilver.net/api/v1/file/95ab4b0b-119b-4330-9392-f767d35ad2a7.xlsx (rawpolls, 2.05 MB) and https://www.natesilver.net/api/v1/file/7bd65470-3e0d-4c0f-a658-22ca23b216ae.xlsx (pollster stats, 132 KB)`
- Auth: none — both files fetched anonymously at HTTP 200 with correct xlsx content-type | Limits: No key, no rate limit, no paywall on the data: the page explicitly states the data may be 'used free of charge for any purpose' with attribution to Silver Bulletin. (The surrounding newsletter has paid tiers; the two data files do not.) Static files, so requests/day: effectively unlimited — UNKNOWN formal cap. History depth: 1998 to January 2026, ~12,300 polls, deliberately weighted toward recent cycles in the rating model.
- Latency: periodic — roughly annual/semiannual ratings updates (Jun 2024, Feb 2025, Jan 2026) | Format: XLSX bulk (no API)
- Relevance: THE single highest-value feed in this entire domain for prediction markets. A raw poll margin is not a probability; the distribution of historical poll-minus-result errors IS the probability. This file gives you empirical error variance by state, by race type, by pollster, by days-to-election, plus each pollster's systematic partisan bias so you can de-bias a fresh poll before aggregating. Everything downstream — implied probability, edge vs. market, sizing — depends on this error distribution. Without it you are guessing at the variance term.

**fivethirtyeight/data GitHub repo — pollster-ratings/raw_polls.csv and polls/** — FiveThirtyEight (defunct, repo still hosted by ABC on GitHub) `LIVE`

- The archived 538 counterpart to the above, and independently valuable because it is CSV and covers a partly different universe. Verified present via the GitHub contents API: pollster-ratings/raw_polls.csv (4,961,378 bytes) — poll-level result-vs-poll error records; pollster-ratings/pollster-ratings-combined.csv (40,046 bytes); plus per-year subfolders 2014-2023. Also polls/pres_pollaverages_1968-2016.csv (50.4 MB) and polls/pres_primary_avgs_1980-2016.csv (30.1 MB) — historical polling AVERAGES, useful for modelling how averages converge toward the result over the campaign. Repo also holds partisan-lean, election-deniers, forecast-review, state-of-the-polls-2024, redistricting-atlas-data. 17,453 stars, last push 2025-02-25.
- Docs: https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/tree/master/pollster-ratings
- Base: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/pollster-ratings/raw_polls.csv`
- Auth: none for raw.githubusercontent; GitHub API needs a free token for higher limits | Limits: raw.githubusercontent.com has no published per-file rate limit — UNKNOWN exact number. GitHub REST API: 60 requests/hour unauthenticated, 5,000/hour authenticated (I hit the unauthenticated search limit live during this research, so that throttle is real). History depth: raw_polls covers the 538 ratings universe up to the repo's final push, i.e. FROZEN at the 2024 cycle — no 2025 or 2026 polls will ever be added. MIRROR IT LOCALLY; ABC has already deleted the 538 website archives and the standalone pollster-ratings repo.
- Latency: static/frozen — no longer updated | Format: CSV bulk via Git/raw HTTP
- Relevance: Same role as Silver Bulletin rawpolls — historical polling error and pollster bias — but in open CSV, with a different sample and with the long-run presidential polling-average series back to 1968. Use both and compare: where two independently-constructed error datasets disagree about a pollster, that disagreement is itself information about model risk. The 1968-2016 averages file is what you need to estimate how much a lead at T-90 days actually predicts the outcome.

**unitedstates/congress-legislators** — @unitedstates project (public domain, community-maintained) `LIVE`

- The identity crosswalk for US politics. Every member of Congress 1789-present in YAML/JSON/CSV with bioguide, ICPSR, THOMAS, GovTrack, OpenSecrets(CRP), VoteSmart, FEC candidate IDs, Wikipedia/Wikidata IDs, full term history with party, state, district, chamber, start/end dates and party switches. Plus committees-current, committees-historical, committee-membership-current, legislators-district-offices, legislators-social-media, and executive.yaml (presidents/VPs). Verified live: last push 2026-09-03, 2,440 stars, not archived. Files live at the repo root as .yaml (e.g. legislators-current.yaml) — the legislators-current.json path I first tried returns 404.
- Docs: https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators
- Base: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators/main/legislators-current.yaml`
- Auth: none | Limits: No key, no rate limit beyond GitHub's (60/hr unauthenticated API, 5,000/hr authenticated; raw file fetches UNKNOWN cap). History depth: 1789-present, complete. Updated within days of membership changes (resignations, deaths, special-election winners).
- Latency: daily-to-weekly (community commits) | Format: YAML/JSON/CSV bulk via Git
- Relevance: Not a market signal by itself but structurally CORE: it is the join key that lets you connect FEC campaign finance, Voteview roll calls, Congress.gov bills, and polling data about the same person. Without it every other political feed is a separate island. Also directly prices 'will member X resign/retire before D' via term-end and vacancy tracking.

**IPU Parline API (v1)** — Inter-Parliamentary Union `LIVE`

- The global reference on national legislatures: ~600 fields on structure, composition and functioning for 193 parliaments, plus the RESULTS OF ALL PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS SINCE THE 1960s. Endpoints verified live and returning JSON:API: /v1/parliaments (328,689 bytes, meta.total=193), /v1/elections (43,562 bytes), /v1/countries, /v1/chambers. Response carries an explicit Creative Commons licence block and terms-of-use in EN/FR. Includes seat counts, party composition, women's representation, electoral system type, term lengths and dissolution rules.
- Docs: https://data.ipu.org/data-tools/api/ (OpenAPI spec at https://api.data.ipu.org/v1/documentation)
- Base: `https://api.data.ipu.org/v1/`
- Auth: none — fetched anonymously | Limits: No API key, no registration, explicitly published as open data under Creative Commons. Exact requests/day or requests/minute cap: UNKNOWN — none stated in the API docs or in response headers. NOTE the asymmetry I measured: the human website data.ipu.org returns HTTP 403 to non-browser clients while api.data.ipu.org serves cleanly — use the API host, not the site. Default page size observed: 10 rows (row_count=10), paginate with page[size]. History depth: parliamentary election results back to the 1960s.
- Latency: updated on parliamentary events — days to weeks after an election | Format: REST JSON (JSON:API spec, OpenAPI described)
- Relevance: CORE for the entire non-US half of political prediction markets, which is systematically underpriced because the data is hard to get. Prices 'which party wins the most seats in [country]', 'will the government lose a confidence vote', 'when is the next election in X'. The seat-composition and electoral-system fields let you convert a national vote-share poll into a seat distribution — the step most naive international models skip entirely.

**Polymarket — Gamma API + CLOB API** — Polymarket `LIVE`

- Live market prices, order books, trade history, volume, liquidity, resolution criteria and outcome tokens for the largest political prediction market. Gamma serves market/event metadata and discovery; CLOB serves order-book and pricing. Verified live: https://gamma-api.polymarket.com/markets?limit=1 returned HTTP 200, and https://clob.polymarket.com/markets returned 1,823,355 bytes of market data. WebSocket channels exist for real-time book/trade streaming.
- Docs: https://docs.polymarket.com/
- Base: `https://gamma-api.polymarket.com/ (metadata) and https://clob.polymarket.com/ (order book)`
- Auth: none for public read/market data; API key + wallet signing required only for trading | Limits: Public read endpoints require no key. Exact requests/minute cap: UNKNOWN — not stated in a way I could confirm; documented limits apply mainly to authenticated order placement. IMPORTANT ACCESS NOTE measured live: the bare host gamma.polymarket.com failed to connect for me while gamma-api.polymarket.com succeeded — use the -api host. History depth: full trade history per market since that market opened; platform data from 2020.
- Latency: realtime / WebSocket | Format: REST JSON + WebSocket
- Relevance: This IS the market side of the research panel — it supplies the live price against which every model probability is compared to compute edge. Also serves as a cross-market reference: Polymarket-vs-Kalshi price divergence on the same contract is a directly tradeable signal and a sanity check on your own model. Resolution-criteria text is essential for avoiding the classic error of modelling a subtly different question than the one being traded.

**Kalshi Trade API (v2)** — Kalshi (CFTC-regulated US exchange) `LIVE`

- Markets, events, series, order books, trades, candlesticks and settlement data for CFTC-regulated event contracts — including elections, control of Congress, presidential approval thresholds, shutdown/appropriations, Fed and macro, and legislative-passage contracts. Verified live: /trade-api/v2/markets?limit=1 and /trade-api/v2/events?limit=1 both HTTP 200 JSON. WebSocket feed available for real-time book updates.
- Docs: https://trading-api.readme.io/reference/getting-started
- Base: `https://api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2/`
- Auth: none for public market-data reads; RSA key-pair signing required for trading/portfolio endpoints | Limits: Public market data readable without credentials (verified). Exact free-tier requests/second: UNKNOWN — Kalshi publishes tiered rate limits (basic/advanced/premier) that govern authenticated trading; the read-only cap is not clearly stated. History depth: candlesticks and trade history per market since listing; exchange operating since 2021.
- Latency: realtime / WebSocket | Format: REST JSON + WebSocket
- Relevance: The regulated-venue price for US political contracts, and the one whose settlement rules are legally specified. Pair with Polymarket for cross-venue arbitrage detection. Kalshi's approval-rating and economic-release contracts settle on named official sources, which means your model input and the settlement source can be made IDENTICAL — the cleanest possible edge calculation in this whole domain.

**Harvard Dataverse API — MIT Election Data + Science Lab (MEDSL) collection** — Harvard Dataverse / MIT Election Data and Science Lab `LIVE`

- The canonical academic archive of certified US election results: president by county 2000-2024, president by state 1976-2024, US House 1976-present, US Senate 1976-present, state legislative returns, and precinct-level returns for recent cycles — all with consistent candidate/party coding and FIPS identifiers. Verified live: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/dataverses/medsl/contents returned HTTP 200 JSON. The generic search API (/api/search?q=election) also returned 200 with 16.6 KB of results.
- Docs: https://guides.dataverse.org/en/latest/api/
- Base: `https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/`
- Auth: none for public datasets; free API token only needed for restricted files or uploads | Limits: No key required for public data. Exact requests/day: UNKNOWN — Dataverse does not publish a hard public rate limit, though it throttles abusive clients. History depth: presidential county returns 2000-2024, state returns 1976-2024, congressional 1976-present. Files are versioned with DOIs, so you can pin an exact dataset version — valuable for reproducibility of a backtest.
- Latency: periodic — certified results posted weeks-to-months after an election | Format: REST JSON API over CSV/TAB bulk files
- Relevance: This is the GROUND TRUTH denominator. Historical polling error only exists because you can subtract the poll from the certified result — and this is where the certified result comes from, cleanly coded. It also supplies the swing/elasticity priors per county and state that let you extrapolate from partial election-night returns to a projected final margin, which is how you price a live 'who wins' contract at 40% reporting.

#### USEFUL

**GovInfo API** — US Government Publishing Office `LIVE`

- Authenticated full text and metadata for official government publications: BILLS, BILLSTATUS, Congressional Record (daily and bound), CRPT (committee reports), CHRG (hearings), FR (Federal Register), CFR, USCOURTS opinions, PLAW (public laws), STATUTE, CPD (Compilation of Presidential Documents — executive orders and presidential statements), and GAO reports. Verified live: /collections and a BILLS collection query with a date cursor both returned HTTP 200.
- Docs: https://api.govinfo.gov/docs/
- Base: `https://api.govinfo.gov/`
- Auth: free API key (api.data.gov signup); DEMO_KEY works for testing | Limits: 1,000 requests/hour per key — the api.data.gov shared default, confirmed in the api.data.gov developer manual, and shared across all api.data.gov services on the same key. DEMO_KEY measured live: x-ratelimit-limit: 10/hour. GovInfo also publishes free BULK DATA at https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata (BILLSTATUS, BILLS, FR, ECFR as XML) with no key — use this for backfill. History depth: varies by collection; Congressional Record from 1994, bound record and Statutes at Large much deeper.
- Latency: daily | Format: REST JSON + bulk XML/ZIP
- Relevance: The full-text layer under Congress.gov. Where Congress.gov tells you a bill moved, GovInfo gives you the enacted text and the Congressional Record floor colloquy. Useful for 'will the final text contain provision X' contracts and for detecting an amendment that guts a bill while the headline bill still 'passes'. Bulk BILLSTATUS XML is the cheapest way to build a complete local legislative database without burning the hourly quota.

**Regulations.gov API (v4)** — US General Services Administration / eRulemaking Program `LIVE`

- Regulatory dockets, individual documents (proposed rules, final rules, notices, supporting analyses) and every public comment filed, with agency, docket ID, comment open/close dates, comment counts and full comment text and attachments. Verified live: /v4/documents with DEMO_KEY returned HTTP 200.
- Docs: https://open.gsa.gov/api/regulationsgov/
- Base: `https://api.regulations.gov/v4/`
- Auth: free API key (api.data.gov signup); DEMO_KEY works for testing | Limits: 1,000 requests/hour per key — api.data.gov shared default, confirmed in the api.data.gov developer manual. DEMO_KEY measured live: x-ratelimit-limit: 10/hour. Regulations.gov may document its own figure; I did not find one that differed, so treat 1,000/hour as the operative number and UNKNOWN for any endpoint-specific sub-limit. Page size max 250, and deep pagination is capped at 5,000 results per query (documented, not measured) — filter by lastModifiedDate to walk past it. History depth: dockets from roughly 2000 onward.
- Latency: daily | Format: REST JSON
- Relevance: Prices 'will rule X be finalized by D'. The comment-close date is a hard scheduled event and the comment volume is a measurable proxy for political resistance — a rule with 200,000 adverse comments has a materially longer and less certain path to a final rule than one with 40. Complements the Federal Register feed: FR tells you what published, Regulations.gov tells you what the affected industry said about it.

**Open States API (v3)** — Plural / Open States (open-source, Princeton-incubated) `LIVE`

- All 50 state legislatures plus DC and Puerto Rico: bills with actions, sponsors, versions and full text; legislators and their contact/district data; committees; legislative events/hearings; and /people.geo for address-to-legislator lookup. Endpoints confirmed from the official docs: /jurisdictions, /people, /people.geo, /bills, /bills/{jurisdiction}/{session}/{id}, /committees, /events. Verified live: https://v3.openstates.org/jurisdictions returned HTTP 403 without a key, i.e. the service is up and key-gated. Scrapers repo pushed 2026-09-18, so the pipeline is actively maintained.
- Docs: https://docs.openstates.org/api-v3/
- Base: `https://v3.openstates.org/`
- Auth: free API key, required — pass via X-API-KEY header or ?apikey= query param | Limits: CAUTION on this number. The official docs page I fetched confirms the base URL and that keys are required but does NOT state the free quota. The tier figures circulating — default 500 queries/day, bronze 5,000/day, silver 50,000/day — come from an Open States GitHub discussion thread (openstates/issues #205), not from official documentation, and an earlier official blog post said v3 limits were 'not yet determined or enforced'. So: EXACT free-tier limit UNKNOWN; plan for ~500/day and request an increase. Free BULK DATA downloads (CSV/JSON per state per session) exist at https://open.pluralpolicy.com/data/ and are the right path for volume. History depth: varies by state, generally 2009-2011 onward.
- Latency: daily (scraper-driven) | Format: REST JSON + CSV bulk
- Relevance: The only broad free feed for state-level legislative contracts — abortion law, election-administration law, redistricting statutes, state budget deadlines, marijuana and gambling legalization. These state markets are thinly researched precisely because the data is fragmented across 50 sites, which is exactly where a systematic feed creates edge.

**LegiScan API** — LegiScan `LIVE`

- Bills, roll-call votes, sponsors, full bill text, amendments, supplements and session lists for all 50 states, DC and the US Congress — notably including STATE-LEVEL ROLL CALL VOTES, which Open States covers less consistently. Verified live: https://api.legiscan.com/?key=x&op=getSessionList&state=CA returned HTTP 200 with a well-formed JSON error ('Invalid API key format'), proving the service is up and responding in 2026.
- Docs: https://legiscan.com/legiscan
- Base: `https://api.legiscan.com/`
- Auth: free API key via registration (free tier is for non-commercial/public-benefit use; commercial use requires a paid agreement) | Limits: EXACT free-tier quota: UNKNOWN — I could not confirm a published calls/day or calls/month figure from a source I fetched. A monthly query allowance is commonly cited but I will not invent the number. LegiScan also publishes free weekly BULK DATASETS (per-state JSON/CSV archives) at https://legiscan.com/datasets, which avoid the API quota entirely and are the sane integration path. History depth: 2009-present for most states. NOTE the licensing asymmetry: free tier is explicitly non-commercial, so a paid prediction-market product likely needs a commercial agreement — check before building on it.
- Latency: daily; bulk datasets weekly | Format: REST JSON + bulk JSON/CSV archives
- Relevance: The state roll-call data is the differentiator: it lets you build per-legislator defection models for state-level contracts the same way Voteview does for Congress.
